claim: Sex differences in plasma growth hormone (GH) profiles are pulsatile in males and persistent in females.
source: Sex differences in plasma growth hormone (GH) profiles, pulsatile in males and persistent in females, regulate sex differences in hepatic STAT5 activation linked to sex differences in gene expression and liver disease susceptibility
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about GH secretion patterns.

claim: Sex differences in plasma GH profiles regulate sex differences in hepatic STAT5 activation.
source: Sex differences in plasma growth hormone (GH) profiles, pulsatile in males and persistent in females, regulate sex differences in hepatic STAT5 activation linked to sex differences in gene expression and liver disease susceptibility
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known regulatory relationship.

claim: The endogenous male rhythm of plasma GH pulse-stimulated liver STAT5 activation induces dynamic, repeated cycles of chromatin opening and closing at several thousand liver DHS.
source: DNase-I hypersensitivity site (DHS) analysis of liver chromatin accessibility in a cohort of 18 individual male mice established that the endogenous male rhythm of plasma GH pulse-stimulated liver STAT5 activation induces dynamic, repeated cycles of chromatin opening and closing at several thousand liver DHS
evidence: This is a primary finding from DNase-seq analysis of 18 individual male mice.

claim: Pulsatile chromatin opening comprises a novel mechanism conferring male bias to liver chromatin accessibility.
source: the endogenous male rhythm of plasma GH pulse-stimulated liver STAT5 activation induces dynamic, repeated cycles of chromatin opening and closing at several thousand liver DHS and comprises a novel mechanism conferring male bias to liver chromatin accessibility
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the DNase-seq analysis.

claim: A single physiological replacement dose of GH given to hypophysectomized male mice restored liver STAT5 activity within 30 min.
source: a single physiological replacement dose of GH given to hypophysectomized male mice restored, within 30 min, liver STAT5 activity and chromatin accessibility at 83% of the dynamic, pituitary hormone-dependent male-biased DHS
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the hypophysectomy and GH replacement study.

claim: A single physiological replacement dose of GH given to hypophysectomized male mice restored chromatin accessibility at 83% of the dynamic, pituitary hormone-dependent male-biased DHS within 30 min.
source: a single physiological replacement dose of GH given to hypophysectomized male mice restored, within 30 min, liver STAT5 activity and chromatin accessibility at 83% of the dynamic, pituitary hormone-dependent male-biased DHS
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the GH replacement experiment.

claim: Dynamic male-biased DHS adopt a bivalent-like epigenetic state in female liver.
source: Dynamic but not static male-biased DHS adopt a bivalent-like epigenetic state in female liver
evidence: This is stated as a finding from chromatin state analysis.

claim: Static female-biased DHS adopt a bivalent-like epigenetic state in male liver.
source: as do static female-biased DHS in male liver, albeit using distinct repressive histone marks in each sex, namely, H3K9me3 at male-biased DHS in female liver and H3K27me3 at female-biased DHS in male liver
evidence: This is stated as a finding from histone mark analysis.

claim: H3K9me3 repressive marks are enriched at male-biased DHS in female liver.
source: Dynamic but not static male-biased DHS adopt a bivalent-like epigenetic state in female liver, as do static female-biased DHS in male liver, albeit using distinct repressive histone marks in each sex, namely, H3K9me3 at male-biased DHS in female liver and H3K27me3 at female-biased DHS in male liver
evidence: This is a specific finding about histone marks at male-biased DHS in female liver.

claim: H3K27me3 repressive marks are enriched at female-biased DHS in male liver.
source: Dynamic but not static male-biased DHS adopt a bivalent-like epigenetic state in female liver, as do static female-biased DHS in male liver, albeit using distinct repressive histone marks in each sex, namely, H3K9me3 at male-biased DHS in female liver and H3K27me3 at female-biased DHS in male liver
evidence: This is a specific finding about histone marks at female-biased DHS in male liver.

claim: Sex-biased H3K36me3 marks are uniquely enriched at static sex-biased DHS.
source: Moreover, sex-biased H3K36me3 marks are uniquely enriched at static sex-biased DHS
evidence: This is stated as a finding from histone mark enrichment analysis.

claim: Sex-biased H3K36me3 marks may serve to keep sex-dependent hepatocyte enhancers free of H3K27me3 repressive marks and thus constitutively open.
source: Moreover, sex-biased H3K36me3 marks are uniquely enriched at static sex-biased DHS, which may serve to keep these sex-dependent hepatocyte enhancers free of H3K27me3 repressive marks and thus constitutively open
evidence: This is stated as a speculative mechanism based on the H3K36me3 enrichment finding.

claim: GH regulates hepatic expression of enzymes and transporters that play critical roles in lipid metabolism.
source: Growth hormone (GH) regulates hepatic expression of enzymes and transporters that play critical roles in lipid metabolism (Vázquez-Borrego et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: GH regulates hepatic expression of enzymes and transporters involved in the detoxification of many drugs and other lipophilic foreign chemicals.
source: Growth hormone (GH) regulates hepatic expression of enzymes and transporters that play critical roles in lipid metabolism (Vázquez-Borrego et al., 2021) and in the detoxification of many drugs and other lipophilic foreign chemicals (Waxman and Holloway, 2009)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Dysregulation of hepatic GH signaling can lead to liver metabolic disorders, including the development of fatty liver disease and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis.
source: Dysregulation of hepatic GH signaling can lead to liver metabolic disorders, including the development of fatty liver disease and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, with males more susceptible than females, as seen in both mice and humans (Dichtel et al., 2022; Kaltenecker et al., 2019; Oxley et al., 2023)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Males are more susceptible than females to fatty liver disease and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis in both mice and humans.
source: Dysregulation of hepatic GH signaling can lead to liver metabolic disorders, including the development of fatty liver disease and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, with males more susceptible than females, as seen in both mice and humans (Dichtel et al., 2022; Kaltenecker et al., 2019; Oxley et al., 2023)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the sex difference in disease susceptibility.

claim: GH regulates many liver-expressed genes in a sex-dependent manner.
source: Correspondingly, GH regulates many liver-expressed genes in a sex-dependent manner, enabling each sex to meet its specific metabolic and hormonal requirements (Wauthier et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Sex-dependent gene expression is controlled by the sex-dependent temporal patterns of pituitary GH secretion.
source: This program of sex-dependent gene expression is controlled by the sex-dependent temporal patterns of pituitary GH secretion (Brie et al., 2019; Farhy et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Sex-dependent temporal patterns of pituitary GH secretion emerge at puberty but are programmed earlier in life by neonatal exposure to androgen.
source: This program of sex-dependent gene expression is controlled by the sex-dependent temporal patterns of pituitary GH secretion (Brie et al., 2019; Farhy et al., 2007), which emerge at puberty but are programmed earlier in life by neonatal exposure to androgen (Chowen et al., 1996; Ramirez et al., 2010; Waxman et al., 1985)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the developmental programming claim.

claim: Pituitary GH secretion and plasma GH profiles are intermittent (pulsatile) in pubertal and adult males.
source: Pituitary GH secretion and, consequently, plasma GH profiles are intermittent (pulsatile) in pubertal and adult males, whereas they are near-continuous (persistent) in pubertal and adult females, as seen in rats, mice, and humans (Waxman and O'Connor, 2006)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the sex difference in GH secretion patterns.

claim: Pituitary GH secretion and plasma GH profiles are near-continuous (persistent) in pubertal and adult females.
source: Pituitary GH secretion and, consequently, plasma GH profiles are intermittent (pulsatile) in pubertal and adult males, whereas they are near-continuous (persistent) in pubertal and adult females, as seen in rats, mice, and humans (Waxman and O'Connor, 2006)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the sex difference in GH secretion patterns.

claim: Plasma GH profiles regulate sex-specific gene transcription in the liver through both positive regulatory mechanisms (class I sex-biased genes) and negative regulatory mechanisms (class II sex-biased genes).
source: These plasma GH profiles, in turn, regulate sex-specific gene transcription in the liver through both positive regulatory mechanisms (class I sex-biased genes) and negative regulatory mechanisms (class II sex-biased genes) (Wauthier et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the classification of sex-biased genes.

claim: The sex-dependent hepatic actions of GH require the transcription factor STAT5.
source: The sex-dependent hepatic actions of GH require the transcription factor STAT5 (Clodfelter et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the requirement for STAT5.

claim: STAT5 is activated by phosphorylation on a single tyrosine residue catalyzed by the GH receptor-associated tyrosine kinase JAK2.
source: The sex-dependent hepatic actions of GH require the transcription factor STAT5 (Clodfelter et al., 2006), which is activated by phosphorylation on a single tyrosine residue catalyzed by the GH receptor-associated tyrosine kinase JAK2 (Waters, 2016)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the mechanism of STAT5 activation.

claim: Each successive male plasma GH pulse induces a cycle of STAT5 tyrosine phosphorylation, dimerization, and nuclear translocation, followed by tyrosine dephosphorylation and recycling of STAT5 back to the cytosol.
source: Each successive male plasma GH pulse induces a cycle of STAT5 tyrosine phosphorylation, dimerization, and nuclear translocation, followed by tyrosine dephosphorylation and recycling of STAT5 back to the cytosol in time to reset the overall signaling pathway for the next plasma GH pulse (Waxman and Holloway, 2009)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the cyclical nature of STAT5 activation.

claim: In male mouse liver, GH pulse-activated STAT5 binds to the DNA motif TTCNNNGAA at genomic sites strongly enriched for proximity to male-biased genes.
source: In male mouse liver, GH pulse-activated STAT5 binds to the DNA motif TTCNNNGAA at genomic sites strongly enriched for proximity to male-biased genes (Zhang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the STAT5 binding pattern.

claim: In female liver, persistent activation of STAT5 by the near-continuous presence of circulating GH is associated with a significant enrichment of STAT5 binding nearby female-biased genes.
source: In female liver, persistent activation of STAT5 by the near-continuous presence of circulating GH is associated with a significant enrichment of STAT5 binding nearby female-biased genes (Zhang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the STAT5 binding pattern in female liver.

claim: Liver STAT5 is activated by male plasma GH pulses within minutes, enabling STAT5 to rapidly induce the transcription of several male-biased genes.
source: Liver STAT5 is activated by male plasma GH pulses within minutes, enabling STAT5 to rapidly induce the transcription of several male-biased genes (Connerney et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the rapid activation of STAT5.

claim: A majority of male-biased genes respond slowly to the feminization of GH secretory patterns.
source: however, a majority of male-biased genes respond slowly to the feminization of GH secretory patterns (Lau-Corona et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the slow response of male-biased genes.

claim: The slow response of male-biased genes to feminization of GH secretory patterns likely reflects the time required for secondary changes, including changes in histone modifications and the underlying chromatin state.
source: however, a majority of male-biased genes respond slowly to the feminization of GH secretory patterns (Lau-Corona et al., 2017), which likely reflects the time required for secondary changes, including changes in histone modifications and the underlying chromatin state (Sugathan and Waxman, 2013)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the inference about the mechanism of slow response.

claim: Continuous infusion of GH in male mice overrides the endogenous plasma GH pulses and substantially feminizes liver gene expression over a period of days.
source: Thus, continuous infusion of GH in male mice overrides the endogenous plasma GH pulses and substantially feminizes liver gene expression over a period of days, with female-biased genes already in an active chromatin state in male liver often responding earlier than genes in an inactive chromatin state (Lau-Corona et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the effect of continuous GH infusion.

claim: DNase-seq has identified ~70,000 DHS in male and female mouse liver.
source: These DHS can be discovered by DNase-seq, which has identified ~70,000 DHS in male and female mouse liver (Ling et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the number of DHS identified.

claim: More than 4000 of the 70,000 liver DHS show sex differences in chromatin accessibility.
source: More than 4000 of the 70,000 liver DHS show sex differences in chromatin accessibility, as well as sex-biased binding of STAT5 and other GH-regulated transcription factors (Sugathan and Waxman, 2013; Ling et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the number of sex-biased DHS.

claim: Male-biased transcription factor binding is strongly enriched at male-biased DHS located nearby male-biased genes.
source: Importantly, male-biased transcription factor binding is strongly enriched at male-biased DHS located nearby male-biased genes, and female-biased transcription factor binding is strongly enriched at female-biased DHS found nearby female-biased genes
evidence: This is stated as an important finding about transcription factor binding patterns.

claim: Female-biased transcription factor binding is strongly enriched at female-biased DHS found nearby female-biased genes.
source: Importantly, male-biased transcription factor binding is strongly enriched at male-biased DHS located nearby male-biased genes, and female-biased transcription factor binding is strongly enriched at female-biased DHS found nearby female-biased genes
evidence: This is stated as an important finding about transcription factor binding patterns.

claim: Sex differences in chromatin structure and accessibility are key features of sex-differential liver gene expression.
source: Sex differences in chromatin structure and accessibility are thus key features of sex-differential liver gene expression (Lau-Corona et al., 2017; Sugathan and Waxman, 2013)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the importance of chromatin differences.

claim: More than 800 male-biased enhancer DHS regions undergo dynamic cycles of male liver chromatin opening and closing.
source: We identify more than 800 male-biased enhancer DHS regions, where the direct binding of plasma GH pulse-activated STAT5 induces a dynamic cycle of male liver chromatin opening and closing at sites that comprise 31% of all male-biased DHS
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding from the study.

claim: Dynamic male-biased DHS comprise 31% of all male-biased DHS.
source: We identify more than 800 male-biased enhancer DHS regions, where the direct binding of plasma GH pulse-activated STAT5 induces a dynamic cycle of male liver chromatin opening and closing at sites that comprise 31% of all male-biased DHS
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: The pulsatility of plasma GH stimulation per se confers significant male bias in chromatin accessibility at a substantial fraction of the genomic sites linked to male-biased liver gene expression.
source: Thus, the pulsatility of plasma GH stimulation per se confers significant male bias in chromatin accessibility, and of STAT5 binding, at a substantial fraction of the genomic sites linked to male-biased liver gene expression
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings about dynamic chromatin opening.

claim: More than 85% of sex-biased DHS are classified as enhancers or weak enhancers in mouse liver.
source: These sex-biased DHS regions were enriched for enhancer histone marks, with >85% classified as enhancers or weak enhancers in mouse liver, compared to 66% for all sex-independent DHS
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 66% of sex-independent DHS are classified as enhancers or weak enhancers.
source: These sex-biased DHS regions were enriched for enhancer histone marks, with >85% classified as enhancers or weak enhancers in mouse liver, compared to 66% for all sex-independent DHS (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Sex-biased DHS were highly enriched for mapping to genes showing a corresponding sex bias in their level of transcription.
source: Assignment of the sex-biased liver DHS to their putative gene targets (closest RefSeq gene or multi-exonic lncRNA gene transcription start site in the same topologically associating domain [TAD]) (Matthews and Waxman, 2018) revealed that sex-biased DHS were highly enriched for mapping to genes showing a corresponding sex bias in their level of transcription, but not for genes whose expression shows the opposite sex bias
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the gene target assignment analysis.

claim: A majority of sex-biased DHS classified as enhancers or insulators are distal to their target genes.
source: Cumulative plots of the distance from each DHS to its target gene revealed that a majority of sex-biased DHS classified as enhancers or insulators are distal to their target genes, whereas sex-biased DHS with H3K4me3 marks, which comprise only 1–2% of all sex-biased DHS, are proximal to their target genes, validating their classification as promoter DHS (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sex-biased DHS with H3K4me3 marks comprise only 1–2% of all sex-biased DHS and are proximal to their target genes.
source: Cumulative plots of the distance from each DHS to its target gene revealed that a majority of sex-biased DHS classified as enhancers or insulators are distal to their target genes, whereas sex-biased DHS with H3K4me3 marks, which comprise only 1–2% of all sex-biased DHS, are proximal to their target genes, validating their classification as promoter DHS (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A majority of sex-biased DHS have the marks of positively acting distal enhancers.
source: Thus, a majority of sex-biased DHS have the marks of positively acting distal enhancers, consistent with our finding that sex-dependent DNA looping at an intra-TAD scale is common in mouse liver (Matthews and Waxman, 2020)
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the DHS classification and distance analysis, with a citation to support the DNA looping finding.

claim: Of the 21 livers analyzed, 10 had high STAT5 EMSA activity (STAT5-high-activity livers) and 11 had very low or no detectable STAT5 EMSA activity (STAT5-low-activity livers).
source: Of the 21 livers, 10 had high STAT5 EMSA activity (STAT5-high-activity livers) and 11 had very low or no detectable STAT5 EMSA activity (STAT5-low-activity livers) (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 18 of the 21 livers gave patterns of DNase-released fragments that correlate with STAT5 activity.
source: Principal component analysis using either the top 200 or the top 600 most significant diffReps-identified differentially accessible regions revealed that 18 of the 21 livers gave patterns of DNase-released fragments that correlate with STAT5 activity
evidence: This is stated as a finding from principal component analysis.

claim: Two of the STAT5-high livers and one of the STAT5-low livers were outliers.
source: Two of the STAT5-high livers and one of the STAT5-low livers were outliers (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: diffReps analysis identified n = 2832 genomic sites where chromatin opening is associated with high liver STAT5 activity.
source: We thus identified n = 2832 genomic sites where chromatin opening is associated with high liver STAT5 activity and n = 123 other sites where chromatin opening is associated with low liver STAT5 activity (Supplementary file 5A)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from diffReps analysis.

claim: diffReps analysis identified n = 123 genomic sites where chromatin opening is associated with low liver STAT5 activity.
source: We thus identified n = 2832 genomic sites where chromatin opening is associated with high liver STAT5 activity and n = 123 other sites where chromatin opening is associated with low liver STAT5 activity (Supplementary file 5A)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from diffReps analysis.

claim: 31% (n = 834) of the 2729 male-biased liver DHS are STAT5-high sites that respond dynamically to the pulsatile activation of liver STAT5 by endogenous male plasma GH pulses.
source: A comparison of the set of 2832 STAT5-high genomic sites with our standard reference set of 70,211 liver DHS revealed that 31% (n = 834) of the 2729 male-biased liver DHS described above are STAT5-high sites, that is, they respond dynamically to the pulsatile activation of liver STAT5 by endogenous male plasma GH pulses
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparison of STAT5-high sites with the reference DHS set.

claim: Only 0.5% of female-biased liver DHS showed dynamic response to STAT5.
source: In contrast, only 0.5% of female-biased liver DHS and 2% of sex-independent liver DHS showed this dynamic response to STAT5 (Figure 2F, green)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Only 2% of sex-independent liver DHS showed dynamic response to STAT5.
source: In contrast, only 0.5% of female-biased liver DHS and 2% of sex-independent liver DHS showed this dynamic response to STAT5 (Figure 2F, green)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: GH pulse-induced chromatin opening at male-biased DHS is enriched 12.9-fold compared to sex-independent DHS (p<1E-05).
source: This strong enrichment of GH/STAT5 pulse-induced chromatin opening at male-biased DHS compared to sex-independent DHS (ES = 12.9; p<1E-05) identifies intermittent chromatin opening induced by male plasma GH pulses as a mechanism that can explain the male bias in chromatin accessibility for a significant subset (31%) of male-biased DHS
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding with statistical significance.

claim: STAT5-high livers showed up to a 2.8-fold higher level of chromatin opening at male-biased DHS that bind STAT5 compared to STAT5-low male livers and female livers.
source: STAT5-high livers showed the highest mean level of chromatin opening, followed by up to a 2.8-fold lower level of chromatin opening at those same genomic regions in STAT5-low male livers and in female livers (Figure 3A, plot 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A, plot 1.

claim: Male-biased DHS that did not bind STAT5 showed nearly equal chromatin accessibility in STAT5-high vs. STAT5-low male livers but approximately twofold lower accessibility in female livers.
source: In contrast, male-biased DHS that did not bind STAT5 (n = 1422 DHS) showed nearly equal chromatin accessibility in STAT5-high vs. STAT5-low male livers but approximately twofold lower accessibility in female livers (Figure 3A, plot 2)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A, plot 2.

claim: STAT5 binding is associated with an open chromatin state.
source: We conclude that STAT5 binding is associated with an open chromatin state, and that STAT5-associated dynamic chromatin opening and closing is a defining characteristic of a specific subset of male-biased DHS but occurs infrequently at female-biased and sex-independent DHS
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the chromatin accessibility analysis.

claim: STAT5-associated dynamic chromatin opening and closing is a defining characteristic of a specific subset of male-biased DHS but occurs infrequently at female-biased and sex-independent DHS.
source: We conclude that STAT5 binding is associated with an open chromatin state, and that STAT5-associated dynamic chromatin opening and closing is a defining characteristic of a specific subset of male-biased DHS but occurs infrequently at female-biased and sex-independent DHS
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the chromatin accessibility analysis.

claim: Dynamic male-biased DHS were enriched for the enhancer state E9 in female liver (ES = 2.42, p=1.6E-69).
source: Dynamic male-biased DHS were enriched for the enhancer state E9 in female liver (ES = 2.42, p=1.6E-69; Figure 7B) but not male liver (Figure 7A)
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical significance and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 81% of the 834 dynamic male-biased DHS contained a STAT5 motif vs. only 38% of the 1895 static male-biased DHS.
source: The presence of a canonical STAT5 motif, TTCNNNGAA, is a distinguishing feature of dynamic male-biased DHS: 81% of the 834 dynamic male-biased DHS contained a STAT5 motif vs. only 38% of the 1895 static male-biased DHS (c.f., 25% background motif frequency at 64,584 sex-independent static DHS) (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 25% of sex-independent static DHS contain a STAT5 motif (background frequency).
source: The presence of a canonical STAT5 motif, TTCNNNGAA, is a distinguishing feature of dynamic male-biased DHS: 81% of the 834 dynamic male-biased DHS contained a STAT5 motif vs. only 38% of the 1895 static male-biased DHS (c.f., 25% background motif frequency at 64,584 sex-independent static DHS) (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: STAT5 binding occurs at a greater fraction of dynamic than static male-biased DHS (85% vs. 32%).
source: Consistent with this, STAT5 binding, determined experimentally by ChIP-seq, occurs at a greater fraction of dynamic than static male-biased DHS (85% vs. 32%; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The level of STAT5 binding (normalized STAT5 ChIP-seq read counts) was significantly higher at the STAT5-bound subsets of the dynamic vs. static DHS sets.
source: and the level of STAT5 binding (normalized STAT5 ChIP-seq read counts) was significantly higher at the STAT5-bound subsets of the dynamic vs. static DHS sets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pulsatile chromatin opening occurred at 124 male-biased DHS (15% of all dynamic male-biased DHS) that did not bind STAT5.
source: Nevertheless, pulsatile chromatin opening was also found at 124 male-biased DHS (15% of all dynamic male-biased DHS) that did not bind STAT5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, plot 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, plot 1B.

claim: 90% of all sex-independent DHS that bind STAT5 do not undergo dynamic chromatin opening and closing.
source: Moreover, STAT5 binding alone is not sufficient to ensure dynamic, male-biased chromatin opening and closing, insofar as 90% of all sex-independent DHS that bind STAT5 do not undergo dynamic chromatin opening and closing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, plot 5A [11,473 sites, 90.3%] vs. 4A [1239 sites, 9.7%])
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only 54% of male-biased DHS that bind STAT5 are dynamic DHS (710 sites), the other 46% (597 sites) being static male-biased DHS.
source: Furthermore, only 54% of male-biased DHS that bind STAT5 are dynamic DHS (710 sites), the other 46% (597 sites) being static male-biased DHS, even though they bind STAT5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, plot 1A vs. 2A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dynamic DHS showed a strong preference for male-biased chromatin accessibility, with the occurrence of STAT5-associated dynamic chromatin opening being 5.6-fold greater at the STAT5-bound male-biased DHS (54%) than at the STAT5-bound sex-independent DHS (9.7%).
source: Finally, dynamic DHS showed a strong preference for male-biased chromatin accessibility, with the occurrence of STAT5-associated dynamic chromatin opening being 5.6-fold greater at the STAT5-bound male-biased DHS (54%) than at the STAT5-bound sex-independent DHS (9.7%)
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding comparing dynamic chromatin opening at different DHS sets.

claim: Male-biased BCL6 binding was significantly enriched at the set of dynamic male-biased DHS (ES = 2.0, p=E-14).
source: Thus, male-biased BCL6 binding was significantly enriched at the set of dynamic male-biased DHS (ES = 2.0, p=E-14) but showed minimal enrichment at static male-biased DHS (ES = 1.3, p=1.6E-04)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from transcription factor binding enrichment analysis.

claim: Male-biased BCL6 binding showed minimal enrichment at static male-biased DHS (ES = 1.3, p=1.6E-04).
source: Thus, male-biased BCL6 binding was significantly enriched at the set of dynamic male-biased DHS (ES = 2.0, p=E-14) but showed minimal enrichment at static male-biased DHS (ES = 1.3, p=1.6E-04)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from transcription factor binding enrichment analysis.

claim: CUX2 was most highly enriched for binding in female liver at genomic sites that correspond to static male-biased DHS (ES = 4.6, p=E-40).
source: In contrast, CUX2 was most highly enriched for binding in female liver at genomic sites that correspond to static male-biased DHS (ES = 4.6, p=E-40), and de novo motif discovery identified a CUX2 motif as the top enriched motif in this, but not the other DHS sets (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Male-biased STAT5 binding sites showed 2.5-fold greater enrichment at dynamic than at static male-biased DHS (ES = 58, p=E-301 vs. ES = 24, p=E-190).
source: Finally, male-biased STAT5 binding sites showed 2.5-fold greater enrichment at dynamic than at static male-biased DHS (ES = 58, p=E-301 vs. ES = 24, p=E-190) (Supplementary file 7B)
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from STAT5 binding enrichment analysis.

claim: Male-biased binding sites for FOXA1 showed enrichment at male-biased DHS with ES = 6.1 at static DHS vs. ES = 3.7 at dynamic DHS.
source: Male-biased binding sites discovered for each FOXA factor showed strong enrichment for binding at male-biased DHS, with up to 2-fold higher enrichments seen at the static male-biased DHS (for FOXA1: ES = 6.1 [static DHS] vs. ES = 3.7 [dynamic DHS]; for FOXA2: ES = 44 [static DHS] vs. ES = 21 [dynamic DHS]) (Table 1, Supplementary files 7B and 8)
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from FOXA1 binding enrichment analysis.

claim: Male-biased binding sites for FOXA2 showed enrichment at male-biased DHS with ES = 44 at static DHS vs. ES = 21 at dynamic DHS.
source: Male-biased binding sites discovered for each FOXA factor showed strong enrichment for binding at male-biased DHS, with up to 2-fold higher enrichments seen at the static male-biased DHS (for FOXA1: ES = 6.1 [static DHS] vs. ES = 3.7 [dynamic DHS]; for FOXA2: ES = 44 [static DHS] vs. ES = 21 [dynamic DHS]) (Table 1, Supplementary files 7B and 8)
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from FOXA2 binding enrichment analysis.

claim: Female-biased FOXA2 binding sites showed strong enrichment for static female-biased DHS (ES = 18, p=E-75).

evidence: This is stated as a finding from FOXA2 binding enrichment analysis.

claim: Hypophysectomy induced changes in chromatin accessibility at several thousand sites.
source: Hypophysectomy induced changes in chromatin accessibility at several thousand sites, including large numbers of sex-independent DHS, with many more genomic regions undergoing chromatin closing than chromatin opening in male liver, but not in female liver (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 5)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Male-biased DHS that responded to hypophysectomy were almost exclusively closed in male liver following hypophysectomy.
source: Importantly, male-biased DHS that responded to hypophysectomy were almost exclusively closed in male liver following hypophysectomy (Figure 4C, first two rows, % opening vs. % closing)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A much smaller percentage of static female-biased DHS responded to hypophysectomy, and the responses observed generally involved chromatin closing in female liver and chromatin opening in male liver.
source: A much smaller percentage of static female-biased DHS responded to hypophysectomy, and the responses observed generally involved chromatin closing in female liver and chromatin opening in male liver (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DHS that close in male liver following hypophysectomy showed strong, specific enrichment (ES = 5.7, p=1.3E-69) for mapping to class I male-specific genes.
source: Supporting this proposal, the DHS that close in male liver following hypophysectomy showed strong, specific enrichment (ES = 5.7, p=1.3E-69) for mapping to class I male-specific genes, which are downregulated in hypox male liver
evidence: This is stated as a finding from enrichment analysis of hypophysectomy-responsive DHS.

claim: DHS that close in hypox female liver showed strong, specific enrichment (ES = 7.8, p=6.6E-46) for mapping to class I female-specific genes.
source: whereas the DHS that close in hypox female liver showed strong, specific enrichment (ES = 7.8, p=6.6E-46) for mapping to class I female-specific genes, which are downregulated in hypox female liver (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from enrichment analysis of hypophysectomy-responsive DHS.

claim: DHS that open in hypox male liver were specifically enriched for mapping to class II female-specific genes (ES = 3.6, p=1.8E-15).
source: In contrast, the DHS that open in hypox male liver were specifically enriched for mapping to class II female-specific genes (ES = 3.6, p=1.8E-15), which are upregulated (de-repressed) in male liver following hypophysectomy
evidence: This is stated as a finding from enrichment analysis of hypophysectomy-responsive DHS.

claim: DHS that open in hypox female liver were enriched for mapping to class II male-specific genes (ES = 1.9, p=4.8E-04).
source: whereas the DHS that open in hypox female liver were specifically enriched albeit only moderately (ES = 1.9, p=4.8E-04) for mapping to class II male-specific genes, which are upregulated in female liver following hypophysectomy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from enrichment analysis of hypophysectomy-responsive DHS.

claim: Exogenous GH treatment induces chromatin opening within 30 min at more than 3500 DHS.
source: Figure 4B shows that exogenous GH treatment induces chromatin opening within 30 min at more than 3500 DHS, including 71% of the 1487 dynamic DHS that closed in male liver following hypophysectomy (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Exogenous GH treatment reopens chromatin at 71% of the 1487 dynamic DHS that closed in male liver following hypophysectomy within 30 min.
source: Figure 4B shows that exogenous GH treatment induces chromatin opening within 30 min at more than 3500 DHS, including 71% of the 1487 dynamic DHS that closed in male liver following hypophysectomy (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The fraction of reopening chromatin regions increased to 83% when considering the set of male-biased dynamic DHS that closed following hypophysectomy.
source: The fraction of reopening chromatin regions increased to 83% when considering the set of male-biased dynamic DHS that closed following hypophysectomy (Supplementary file 1A, column AK)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the GH replacement experiment.

claim: Chromatin reopening was sustained for at least 90 min and then decreased substantially back toward baseline by 240 min.
source: Chromatin reopening was sustained for at least 90 min and then decreased substantially back toward baseline by 240 min (Figure 4B; see Figure 5A, plot 1), at which time liver STAT5 signaling has terminated (Connerney et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B and Figure 5A, plot 1, with a citation for STAT5 signaling termination.

claim: The mean level of chromatin reopening induced by an exogenous GH pulse at dynamic male-biased DHS was very similar to that of the same DHS set in STAT5-high male liver.
source: Importantly, the mean level of chromatin reopening induced by an exogenous GH pulse at dynamic male-biased DHS was very similar to that of the same DHS set in STAT5-high male liver (Figure 5A, plot 1 vs. Figure 3A, plot 5; peak DNase-I activity value 1886 vs. 1848)
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 5A, plot 1 and Figure 3A, plot 5.

claim: Male-biased enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1) were strongly enriched at both dynamic and static male-biased DHS compared to a background set of 64,584 static, sex-independent DHS.
source: Male-biased enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1) were strongly enriched at both dynamic and static male-biased DHS compared to a background set of 64,584 static, sex-independent DHS (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 7B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Male-biased H3K36me3 marks were enriched at static but not at dynamic male-biased DHS.
source: In contrast, male-biased H3K36me3 marks, which are characteristic of transcribed regions but have also been shown to inhibit the spread of PRC2-catalyzed H3K27me3 repressive marks (Yuan et al., 2011), were enriched at static but not at dynamic male-biased DHS
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation for the function of H3K36me3 marks.

claim: Static but not dynamic male-biased DHS were significantly depleted of female-biased enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1).
source: In addition, static but not dynamic male-biased DHS were significantly depleted of female-biased enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1) (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Static female-biased DHS showed strong enrichments for female-biased enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1), female-biased H3K4me3 promoter marks, and female-biased H3K36me3 transcribed region marks.
source: Static female-biased DHS showed strong enrichments for female-biased enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1), female-biased H3K4me3 promoter marks, and female-biased H3K36me3 transcribed region marks (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Female-biased H3K9me3 repressive marks were significantly enriched at both dynamic and static male-biased DHS.
source: In contrast, female-biased H3K9me3 repressive marks were significantly enriched at both dynamic and static male-biased DHS (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was no corresponding enrichment of male-biased H3K9me3 marks at female-biased DHS.
source: however, we did not find any corresponding enrichment of male-biased H3K9me3 marks at female-biased DHS
evidence: This is stated as a finding from histone mark enrichment analysis.

claim: H3K9me3 marks are specifically used to repress male-biased genes in female liver.
source: This novel finding suggests that H3K9me3 marks are specifically used to repress male-biased genes in female liver, contrasting with the specific use of H3K27me3 marks to repress female-biased genes in male liver
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the histone mark enrichment findings.

claim: H3K27me3 marks are specifically used to repress female-biased genes in male liver.
source: This novel finding suggests that H3K9me3 marks are specifically used to repress male-biased genes in female liver, contrasting with the specific use of H3K27me3 marks to repress female-biased genes in male liver
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the histone mark enrichment findings.

claim: Dynamic male-biased DHS were enriched for chromatin state E10 in female liver (ES = 2.89, p=1.9E-18) but not male liver.
source: Dynamic male-biased DHS were also enriched for chromatin state E10 in female liver (ES = 2.89, p=1.9E-18) but not male liver
evidence: This is stated as a finding from chromatin state enrichment analysis.

claim: The genomic regions encompassing dynamic male-biased DHS are in a bivalent-like chromatin state in female liver.
source: This pattern of chromatin state E9 and E10 enrichment at dynamic male-biased DHS in female liver, combined with the strong enrichment of H3K9me3 repressive marks (Figure 6B), indicates that the genomic regions encompassing dynamic male-biased DHS are in a bivalent-like chromatin state in female liver (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from chromatin state and histone mark analysis.

claim: Static female-biased DHS showed little or no enrichment of specific chromatin states in female liver compared to the genome-wide background set of static sex-independent DHS.
source: Static female-biased DHS showed little or no enrichment of specific chromatin states in female liver compared to the genome-wide background set of static sex-independent DHS (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The genomic regions encompassing static female-biased DHS were strongly enriched in male liver for inactive chromatin states E1 (repressive mark H3K27me3), E2, and E4.
source: Indeed, the genomic regions encompassing static female-biased DHS were strongly enriched in male liver for inactive chromatin states E1 (repressive mark H3K27me3), E2, and E4 (Figure 7A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Static female-biased DHS showed moderate enrichment in male liver for enhancer states E10 and E11.
source: Static female-biased DHS showed moderate enrichment in male liver for enhancer states E10 and E11, which are respectively characterized by the active enhancer marks H3K27ac and H3K4me1 but devoid of DHS
evidence: This is stated as a finding from chromatin state enrichment analysis.

claim: Static female-biased DHS showed moderate enrichment in male liver for bivalent state E12.
source: Static female-biased DHS also showed moderate enrichment in male liver for bivalent state E12, which is characterized by a mixture of activating histone marks and the presence of repressive H3K27me3 marks
evidence: This is stated as a finding from chromatin state enrichment analysis.

claim: At least a subset of static female-biased DHS is in a bivalent-like state in male liver.
source: consistent with the strong enrichment of the latter histone mark at static female-biased DHS seen in Figure 6A, above, and the overall conclusion that at least a subset of static female-biased DHS is in a bivalent-like state in male liver
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from chromatin state and histone mark analysis.

claim: Dynamic and static male-biased DHS both showed strong enrichment for mapping to male-biased gene targets (8-fold and 11.7-fold enrichments, respectively).
source: Dynamic and static male-biased DHS both showed strong enrichment for mapping to male-biased gene targets (8-fold and 11.7-fold enrichments, respectively), as did static female-biased DHS for female-biased gene targets (12.5-fold enrichment) when DHS were mapped to the single nearest transcription start site in the same TAD (Supplementary file 1B)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from gene target mapping analysis.

claim: Static female-biased DHS showed strong enrichment for mapping to female-biased gene targets (12.5-fold enrichment).
source: Dynamic and static male-biased DHS both showed strong enrichment for mapping to male-biased gene targets (8-fold and 11.7-fold enrichments, respectively), as did static female-biased DHS for female-biased gene targets (12.5-fold enrichment) when DHS were mapped to the single nearest transcription start site in the same TAD (Supplementary file 1B)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from gene target mapping analysis.

claim: All three sets of sex-biased DHS were significantly enriched for mapping to hypophysectomy class I-responsive sex-biased genes compared to hypophysectomy class II-responsive sex-biased genes.
source: Other analyses revealed that all three sets of sex-biased DHS were significantly enriched for mapping to hypophysectomy class I-responsive sex-biased genes compared to hypophysectomy class II-responsive sex-biased genes (Supplementary file 1B)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from gene target mapping analysis.

claim: Top enriched GO terms common to both dynamic and static male-biased DHS included lipid metabolic process and steroid metabolic process.
source: Top enriched GO terms common to both dynamic and static male-biased DHS included lipid metabolic process and steroid metabolic process, consistent with the major role that GH plays in the male-prevalence of fatty liver development and liver metabolic disease (Dichtel et al., 2022; Kaltenecker et al., 2019; Oxley et al., 2023)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from GO enrichment analysis with citations supporting the biological relevance.

claim: Unique enriched terms for dynamic male-biased DHS included cell adhesion, gland development, and hepatico-biliary development.
source: Unique enriched terms for dynamic male-biased DHS included cell adhesion, gland development, and hepatico-biliary development
evidence: This is stated as a finding from GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Gene targets of static male-biased DHS were uniquely enriched for cellular response to glucocorticoid stimulus and EGF receptor signaling.
source: whereas gene targets of static male-biased DHS were uniquely enriched for cellular response to glucocorticoid stimulus and EGF receptor signaling, among others (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 10, bottom)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Static female-biased DHS gene targets were uniquely enriched for long-chain fatty acid metabolic pathway and related terms.
source: Static female-biased DHS gene targets were uniquely enriched for long-chain fatty acid metabolic pathway and related terms
evidence: This is stated as a finding from GO enrichment analysis.

claim: The set of dynamic sex-independent DHS mapped to gene targets enriched for terms related to glucose transport and metabolism, IGF receptor signaling, and fibroblast proliferation.
source: Finally, the set of dynamic sex-independent DHS mapped to gene targets enriched for terms related to glucose transport and metabolism, IGF receptor signaling, and fibroblast proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from GO enrichment analysis.

claim: GH acts at three distinct steps to regulate sex-dependent hepatocyte gene expression, all three involving the GH-activated transcription factor STAT5.
source: GH thus acts at three distinct steps to regulate sex-dependent hepatocyte gene expression, all three involving the GH-activated transcription factor STAT5 (Figure 8): GH pulse-induced chromatin opening at dynamic male-biased DHS driven by pulsatile GH activation of STAT5, as discussed further below; direct transcriptional activation of sex-biased genes by GH-activated STAT5; and GH/STAT5-dependent transcriptional regulation of downstream repressors, such as the female-specific CUX2, which binds to male-biased enhancers in female liver to reinforce sex differences in gene transcription
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion with reference to Figure 8.

claim: GH pulse-induced chromatin opening in male mouse liver is directly controlled by the endogenous male rhythm of plasma GH stimulation of hepatocytes.
source: GH pulse-induced chromatin opening in male mouse liver is shown to be directly controlled by the endogenous male rhythm of plasma GH stimulation of hepatocytes, the major liver cell type contributing to sex-biased liver gene expression (Goldfarb et al., 2022)
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with a citation supporting the role of hepatocytes.

claim: The GH pulse-regulated chromatin regions responded to changes in plasma GH levels in a rapid and dynamic manner, with extensive GH-induced chromatin opening occurring within 30 min.
source: The GH pulse-regulated chromatin regions identified here responded to changes in plasma GH levels in a rapid and dynamic manner, with extensive GH-induced chromatin opening occurring within 30 min, as seen when hypophysectomized male mice were given a physiological replacement dose of GH pulse by intraperitoneal injection (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the GH replacement experiment.

claim: 85% of the dynamic male-biased DHS identified were bound by STAT5.
source: Importantly, 85% of the dynamic male-biased DHS identified here (710 of 834 dynamic male-biased DHS) were bound by STAT5, which appears to be a key driver of these GH pulse-induced chromatin opening events
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from STAT5 ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: STAT5 appears to be a key driver of GH pulse-induced chromatin opening events.
source: Importantly, 85% of the dynamic male-biased DHS identified here (710 of 834 dynamic male-biased DHS) were bound by STAT5, which appears to be a key driver of these GH pulse-induced chromatin opening events
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the high frequency of STAT5 binding at dynamic male-biased DHS.

claim: Chromatin closing followed the termination of nuclear STAT5 signaling, which is complete within 4 hr.
source: Chromatin closing followed the termination of nuclear STAT5 signaling, which is complete within 4 hr (Connerney et al., 2017) and occurs in sufficient time to reset the GH receptor-JAK2 signaling complex and resensitize hepatocytes before the next plasma GH pulse (Gebert et al., 1997; Figure 2A)
evidence: This is stated with citations supporting the timing of STAT5 signaling termination and receptor resensitization.

claim: The extent of chromatin opening at male-biased DHS in female liver is very similar to the level in livers from male mice euthanized when liver STAT5 activity is low.
source: Indeed, the extent of chromatin opening at these male-biased DHS in female liver is very similar to the level in livers from male mice euthanized when liver STAT5 activity is low, a time inferred to be between plasma GH pulses (STAT5-low male livers; Figure 3A, panel 5)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from chromatin accessibility analysis.

claim: GH pulse-responsive DHS were discovered by comparing global chromatin accessibility patterns in a set of 8 livers collected from mice euthanized at a peak of GH-activated STAT5 DNA-binding activity to those of 10 other livers from mice euthanized between pulses of STAT5 DNA-binding activity.
source: GH pulse-responsive DHS were discovered by comparing global chromatin accessibility patterns in a set of 8 livers collected from mice euthanized at a peak of GH-activated STAT5 DNA-binding activity (STAT5-high livers) to those of 10 other livers from mice euthanized between pulses of STAT5 DNA-binding activity, that is, when liver STAT5 activity is very low or undetectable (STAT5-low livers)
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental design.

claim: The top 200 genomic regions showing differential chromatin opening between STAT5-high and STAT5-low livers also separated a group of nine C57Bl/6 male mouse liver DNase-seq samples from the ENCODE consortium into two distinct classes.
source: Importantly, the top 200 genomic regions showing differential chromatin opening between STAT5-high and STAT5-low livers also separated a group of nine C57Bl/6 male mouse liver DNase-seq samples from the ENCODE consortium into two distinct classes, corresponding to the accessibility patterns of STAT5-high-activity livers (n = 4) and STAT5-low-activity livers (n = 5), respectively
evidence: This is stated as a validation finding using independent ENCODE data.

claim: The plasma GH-induced signaling pathways and downstream epigenetic events leading to dynamic chromatin opening and closing at these specific genomic regions are robust across studies and mouse strains.
source: Thus, the plasma GH-induced signaling pathways and downstream epigenetic events leading to dynamic chromatin opening and closing at these specific genomic regions are robust across studies and mouse strains
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the validation with ENCODE data.

claim: STAT5 may act as a pioneer factor to enable chromatin opening at the Il9 gene locus in Th9 T-cells.
source: This finding is consistent with the proposal that STAT5 acts as a pioneer factor to enable chromatin opening, as was reported for STAT5 action at the Il9 gene locus in Th9 T-cells (Fu et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the pioneer factor role of STAT5.

claim: Static male-biased DHS are relatively deficient in STAT5 binding compared to dynamic male-biased DHS.
source: Static male-biased DHS are relatively deficient in STAT5 binding compared to dynamic male-biased DHS, but showed significant enrichment for binding the female-specific repressor protein CUX2 (Conforto et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from transcription factor binding analysis.

claim: CUX2 binding may contribute to the greater closure of static male-biased DHS in female liver.
source: This binding of CUX2 may contribute to the greater closure of those DHS in female compared to male liver (Figure 3A, plot 6)
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the CUX2 binding enrichment finding.

claim: Static male-biased DHS showed strong enrichment of male-biased binding sites for the pioneer factors FOXA1 and FOXA2.
source: Finally, static male-biased DHS showed strong enrichment of male-biased binding sites for the pioneer factors FOXA1 and FOXA2, which may help maintain their constitutively open chromatin state in male liver
evidence: This is stated as a finding from transcription factor binding analysis.

claim: FOXA1 and FOXA2 may help maintain the constitutively open chromatin state of static male-biased DHS in male liver.
source: Finally, static male-biased DHS showed strong enrichment of male-biased binding sites for the pioneer factors FOXA1 and FOXA2, which may help maintain their constitutively open chromatin state in male liver
evidence: This is stated as a speculative mechanism based on FOXA binding enrichment.

claim: Both dynamic and static male-biased DHS are largely (~95%) promoter-distal enhancer DHS.
source: Both dynamic and static male-biased DHS are largely (~95%) promoter-distal enhancer DHS, as indicated by their flanking histone modifications
evidence: This is stated as a finding from DHS classification analysis.

claim: Sex-dependent intra-TAD DNA looping mechanisms are common in mouse liver.
source: This supports our prior finding that sex-dependent intra-TAD DNA looping mechanisms are common in mouse liver (Matthews and Waxman, 2020)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the DNA looping finding.

claim: A bivalent chromatin state may protect dynamic male-biased DHS from irreversible silencing.
source: A bivalent chromatin state may protect dynamic male-biased DHS from irreversible silencing (Kumar et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated as a speculative mechanism with a citation to support the protective role of bivalent states.

claim: A bivalent chromatin state may confer the potential for chromatin opening leading to activation of latent enhancer activity in female liver in response to chemical exposure or biological stress.
source: and confer the potential for chromatin opening leading to activation of their latent enhancer activity in female liver, for example, in response to chemical exposure or biological stress (Lodato et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated as a speculative mechanism with a citation to support the potential for activation.

claim: H3K36me3 marks are classically associated with the demarcation of actively transcribed genes.
source: H3K36me3 marks are classically associated with the demarcation of actively transcribed genes (Li et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the classical role of H3K36me3 marks.

claim: H3K36me3 marks are used to maintain cell type identity by inhibiting the spread of H3K27me3 repressive marks at cell type-specific enhancers.
source: but are also used to maintain cell type identity by inhibiting the spread of H3K27me3 repressive marks at cell type-specific enhancers (Yuan et al., 2011; Hoetker et al., 2023)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the role of H3K36me3 in maintaining cell identity.

claim: The enrichment of H3K36me3 marks at static male-biased DHS could be an important mechanism to maintain sex-dependent hepatocyte identity by keeping static male-biased enhancers constitutively open and free of H3K27me3 repressive marks in male liver.
source: The enrichment of H3K36me3 marks at static male-biased DHS described here could thus be an important mechanism to maintain sex-dependent hepatocyte identity by keeping static male-biased enhancers constitutively open and free of H3K27me3 repressive marks in male liver, and correspondingly for H3K36me3 marks enriched at static female-biased DHS in female liver
evidence: This is stated as a speculative mechanism based on the H3K36me3 enrichment finding.

claim: A single physiological replacement dose of GH restored liver STAT5 activity and chromatin accessibility at 83% of the dynamic male-biased DHS that closed following hypophysectomy.
source: Strikingly, a single physiological replacement dose of GH restored, within 30 min, liver STAT5 activity and chromatin accessibility at 83% of the dynamic male-biased DHS that closed following hypophysectomy
evidence: This is stated as a striking finding from the GH replacement experiment.

claim: These chromatin sites are maintained in a primed (poised) state in hypox male liver over a period of several weeks.
source: These chromatin sites are maintained in a primed (poised) state in hypox male liver over a period of several weeks, despite the prolonged deficiency of GH and other pituitary hormones, including gonadal steroids, and the dysregulation of several thousand liver-expressed genes (Wauthier et al., 2010; Connerney et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citations supporting the gene dysregulation.

claim: DHS that close in male liver following hypophysectomy are regulatory elements with intrinsic, positively acting enhancer potential.
source: These enrichments are consistent with the definition of class II sex-biased genes, that is, genes that are upregulated by hypophysectomy in the sex where they show lower expression in intact mice. Together, these findings lend strong support for the functional role of each class of sex-biased and pituitary hormone-dependent DHS as regulatory elements with intrinsic, positively acting enhancer potential
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the enrichment analysis of hypophysectomy-responsive DHS.

claim: Testosterone has a well-established role in early postnatal programming of the hypothalamic control of pituitary GH secretory patterns beginning at puberty and lasting through adulthood.
source: Testosterone has a well-established role in early postnatal programming of the hypothalamic control of pituitary GH secretory patterns beginning at puberty and lasting through adulthood (Chowen et al., 1996; Ramirez et al., 2010; Waxman et al., 1985)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the role of testosterone in programming GH secretion.

claim: Plasma GH patterns, and not gonadal steroids, dominate the epigenetic control of liver sex differences.
source: While it is also possible that testosterone, as well as estrogens, could also regulate sex differences in hepatocytes directly at the epigenetic or transcriptional level, our findings support the proposal that plasma GH patterns, and not gonadal steroids, dominate the epigenetic control of liver sex differences
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings about GH-induced chromatin opening.

claim: Hepatocyte-specific knockout of androgen receptor (AR) dysregulates ~15% of sex-biased genes in the liver.
source: On the other hand, it is important to note that hepatocyte-specific knockout of androgen receptor (AR) does, in fact, dysregulate ~15% of sex-biased genes in the liver, albeit with a much lower effect size than global AR knockout (Xiong et al., 2023)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the role of AR in regulating some sex-biased genes.

claim: AR binding sites are enriched at male-biased genes in mouse liver.
source: Supporting this possibility, AR binding sites were recently reported to be enriched at male-biased genes in mouse liver (Rodríguez-Montes et al., 2023)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the enrichment of AR binding at male-biased genes.

claim: Estrogen receptor (ERα) likely plays only a minor role in regulating sex-biased liver DHS enhancers.
source: In contrast, estrogen receptor (ERα) likely plays only a minor role in regulating sex-biased liver DHS enhancers, given the lack of major effect of hepatocyte-specific ERα knockout on sex-biased liver gene expression (Nikkanen et al., 2022)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the minor role of ERα.

claim: Only 12% of static female-biased DHS close in female liver following hypophysectomy.
source: and our finding that only 12% of static female-biased DHS close in female liver following hypophysectomy, despite the decrease in circulating estradiol levels (Wang and Greenwald, 1993)
evidence: This is stated as a finding with a citation supporting the decrease in estradiol levels.
